symptom_text: Anthracnose leaf spot on corn appears as small, oval to irregular water-soaked lesions on leaves that enlarge and develop tan to brown centers with yellow to reddish-brown or dark brown borders, often surrounded by a yellow halo; lesions may coalesce to blight large areas of leaf tissue. The top dieback phase affects the upper stalk and leaves, causing shredding and rotting of the upper plant, with the stalk pith becoming discolored and the outer stalk tissue turning shiny black due to fungal colonization, a hallmark diagnostic feature visible on the stalk surface.

Common rust of corn produces small, circular to elongated, powdery pustules scattered across both upper and lower surfaces of leaves, though they may also appear on husks and leaf sheaths. Early pustules are golden-brown to cinnamon-brown in color, often surrounded by a yellow halo, and rupture through the epidermis to release masses of brick-red to dark brown powdery urediniospores. As the season progresses, pustules darken to a blackish-brown as teliospores form. Lesions are distributed randomly across the leaf blade and can coalesce under heavy infection, giving leaves a scorched, necrotic appearance.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Common rust is caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi Schwein.

affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Pustules occur on both leaf surfaces but are also found on husks and leaf sheaths.

visual_symptoms.value: Small, circular to elongated, brick-red to brown powdery pustules on both leaf surfaces, darkening to black with age
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Pustules are small, circular to elongate, and golden brown to cinnamon brown in color. As the pustules age, they turn dark brown to black.

symptom_text: Common smut of corn, caused by Ustilago maydis, produces distinctive large, irregular galls that can form on any above-ground meristematic tissue including ears, tassels, stalks, and leaves. The galls begin as white to silvery-gray, shiny, smooth-surfaced swellings covered by a thin membrane of host and fungal tissue. As the galls mature, they expand dramatically—sometimes reaching the size of a softball—and the interior fills with a mass of dark olive-brown to black powdery teliospores. At maturity, the outer membrane ruptures, releasing the sooty black spore mass. On ears, individual kernels may be replaced by galls, while on tassels entire florets can be converted into spore-bearing structures. The galls have a spongy to firm texture when young and become dry and papery as they age and burst.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Common smut is caused by the fungus Ustilago maydis (DC.) Corda.

affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Galls can form on any above ground part of the corn plant including the ear, tassel, stalk, and leaves.

visual_symptoms.value: Large white to gray galls that turn black and powdery at maturity as the membrane ruptures and releases dark teliospores
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Galls are white to gray and shiny when young, and turn black and powdery at maturity when the outer membrane breaks open to release the dark mass of spores.

symptom_text: Corn smut is characterized by the formation of large, irregular galls that can appear on any above-ground part of the corn plant, including ears, tassels, stalks, and leaves. These galls begin as white to silvery-gray, shiny, and firm swellings covered by a thin membrane. As the galls mature, they enlarge dramatically—sometimes reaching the size of a softball—and the interior fills with a mass of dark olive-brown to black powdery spores (teliospores). The outer membrane eventually ruptures, releasing the sooty black spore mass. On ears, galls replace individual kernels or entire ear sections, while on tassels and stalks they appear as distorted, tumor-like outgrowths. The contrast between the pale, intact membrane of young galls and the dark, dusty spore mass of ruptured mature galls is the hallmark visual feature of this disease.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Corn smut is caused by the fungus Ustilago maydis (DC) Corda.

affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Galls can form on any above ground part of the plant including the ears, tassels, stalks, and leaves.

visual_symptoms.value: Large galls that are white to gray when young, turning dark brown to black and powdery as spores mature; galls replace kernels on ears and form tumor-like swellings on other plant parts
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Galls are white to gray and shiny when young. As they mature, galls turn dark brown to black and become filled with a powdery mass of spores. Galls can be as large as a softball.

Crazy top of corn, caused by the downy mildew pathogen Sclerophthora macrospora, produces a striking array of visual symptoms concentrated in the upper portions of the plant. Infected plants display excessive tillering at the base and profuse, abnormal branching of the tassel, which becomes massively proliferated into a leafy, brush-like mass of small, distorted leaves rather than normal floral structures — a condition often described as a 'witch's broom' appearance. The upper leaves may be narrow, twisted, and rolled, sometimes showing chlorotic (yellow) streaking. Ears, when present, are often poorly formed or replaced by leafy, proliferated tissue. Affected plants are typically stunted compared to healthy neighbors, and the overall plant architecture appears grossly distorted, with the abnormal tassel proliferation being the most diagnostic and visually distinctive feature.

Diplodia ear rot of corn is characterized by a white to grayish-white, dense mycelial growth that begins at the base of the ear and progresses upward between the husks and kernels. Infected ears appear bleached or straw-colored, with husks tightly adhering to the ear. Small, black fungal fruiting bodies (pycnidia) are embedded in the husks, cob tissue, and kernel surfaces, appearing as raised black dots visible to the naked eye. Kernels become lightweight, chalky, and shrunken, often with a grayish discoloration. The rot typically initiates at the base of the ear and moves toward the tip, resulting in a characteristic basal rot pattern. Affected ears are often lightweight and may be entirely rotted, with the entire ear covered in white mold under humid conditions.

visual_symptoms.value: White mould starting at the ear base, turning grayish-brown; raised black pycnidia on husk or kernels
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: white mold beginning at the base of the ear that eventually becomes grayish-brown and rots the entire ear

symptom_text: Diplodia stalk rot of corn, caused by Stenocarpella maydis, primarily affects the lower internodes and crown of the stalk. Infected stalks exhibit internal discoloration, with the pith turning brown and shredding, leaving only the vascular bundles intact, giving the interior a hollow or pithy appearance. Externally, small black pycnidia (fungal fruiting bodies) may be visible on the lower stalk nodes and internodes, often embedded in the bleached, straw-colored outer rind. Infected plants frequently lodge or fall over as the structural integrity of the stalk is compromised. Symptoms typically appear after silking, beginning at the crown and progressing upward through the lower internodes.

Corn ear rots present as a complex of fungal diseases affecting the ear, cob, and kernels. Gibberella ear rot produces a distinctive pink to reddish mold that typically begins at the ear tip and progresses downward, with kernels becoming discolored and shrunken. Fusarium ear rot appears as white to pink streaks or patches scattered across individual kernels, often with a 'starburst' pattern radiating from the kernel tip. Diplodia ear rot causes a white to grayish-white dense mycelial growth that bleaches the husks and causes kernels to become lightweight, chalky, and firmly adhered to the cob, usually starting at the base of the ear. Aspergillus ear rot is characterized by powdery olive-green to yellow-green spore masses on and between kernels, often associated with insect damage or mechanical injury. Penicillium ear rot shows blue-green to turquoise powdery mold growth between kernels, typically associated with kernel damage or late-season wet conditions.

pathogen.value: Multiple fungi including Gibberella zeae (Fusarium graminearum), Fusarium verticillioides, Diplodia maydis (Stenocarpella maydis), Aspergillus flavus, and Penicillium spp.
pathogen.verbatim_quote: Several different fungi can cause ear rots in corn, including Gibberella zeae (also known as Fusarium graminearum), Fusarium verticillioides (formerly F. moniliforme), Stenocarpella maydis (formerly Diplodia maydis), Aspergillus flavus, and Penicillium species.

visual_symptoms.value: Pink to red mold at ear tip (Gibberella); white to pink starburst kernel discoloration (Fusarium); white-gray bleached husks and chalky kernels from ear base (Diplodia); olive-green powdery spore masses (Aspergillus); blue-green mold between kernels (Penicillium)
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Gibberella ear rot is characterized by a pink to reddish mold that usually starts at the tip of the ear. Fusarium ear rot appears as white to pink mold on individual kernels, often in a 'starburst' pattern. Diplodia ear rot produces a white to grayish-white mold that usually starts at the base of the ear and the kernels become lightweight and chalky. Aspergillus ear rot is identified by an olive-green to yellow-green powdery mold growth on and between kernels.

symptom_text: Corn eyespot appears primarily on leaves as small, circular to oval lesions with a pale yellow or cream-colored center surrounded by a distinct brown ring and a yellow halo, giving each spot the appearance of an eye. Lesions are typically 1–4 mm in diameter and are scattered across the leaf blade, often occurring in large numbers that can coalesce under severe infection, leading to blighting of leaf tissue. The tan to straw-colored necrotic centers are sharply delimited by the darker brown border, and the surrounding chlorotic halo fades gradually into healthy green tissue.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Eyespot of corn is caused by the fungus Aureobasidium zeae (Narita & Hiratsuka) J.M. Dingley (syn. Kabatiella zeae Narita & Hiratsuka).

affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Eyespot lesions are found on leaves.

visual_symptoms.value: Small circular lesions with pale tan centers, brown borders, and yellow halos on leaves
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Lesions are small (1/8 inch diameter), circular, with a pale tan center, brown border, and yellow halo, giving the appearance of an eye.

symptom_text: Fusarium ear rot of corn is characterized by a white to pink or salmon-colored cottony mold that typically begins at the tip of the ear and progresses downward between the kernels. Individual kernels may appear bleached, streaked, or straw-colored, and a white mycelial mat can be observed growing between and over the kernels. Infected kernels are often lightweight, shrunken, and may display a 'starburst' or streaking pattern radiating from the embryo. The disease can also affect stalks, causing internal browning and rotting of the pith tissue, which weakens the stalk and predisposes plants to lodging. Symptoms are most visible on the ear husks and exposed kernel surfaces, with discoloration ranging from white to pink depending on the Fusarium species involved.

pathogen.value: Fusarium verticillioides (formerly F. moniliforme), Fusarium graminearum, and other Fusarium spp.

Goss's Wilt of corn causes large, water-soaked to tan or gray-green leaf lesions with wavy, irregular margins that run parallel to the leaf veins, giving the lesions a freckled appearance due to dark green to black water-soaked spots ('freckles') scattered within the tan necrotic tissue. Infected leaves may display bacterial exudate (dried, shiny, crusty deposits) along the lesion margins. Systemic infection leads to wilting and death of the entire plant, with vascular discoloration visible when stalks are split. Lesions are distributed across the leaf blade and can coalesce to kill large portions of the canopy.

affected_organs.value: Leaves, with systemic infection of the stalk

visual_symptoms.value: Elongated tan to grayish-brown lesions with wavy margins along the veins, carrying diagnostic dark water-soaked 'freckles' that appear translucent when backlit
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Dark green to black, scattered, discontinuous water-soaked spots ("freckles") develop within the plant tissue inside the lesions and are diagnostic for Goss's wilt

symptom_text: Gray leaf spot of corn produces rectangular, tan to gray lesions on the leaves that are sharply delimited by leaf veins, giving them a distinctly blocky or angular appearance. Lesions initially appear as small, necrotic spots with yellow halos that elongate parallel to the leaf veins, eventually turning gray to brown as the fungal sporulation develops on the lesion surface. The lesions are dry and papery in texture, and under humid conditions a grayish, velvety coating of conidia may be visible on both upper and lower leaf surfaces. Severe infections cause lesions to coalesce, leading to large areas of blighted, dead leaf tissue, with symptoms typically appearing first on lower leaves and progressing upward through the canopy.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Gray leaf spot is caused by the fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis.

affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Gray leaf spot lesions are found on the leaves of corn plants.

visual_symptoms.value: Rectangular, tan to gray, vein-delimited lesions that are initially small with yellow halos, elongating parallel to leaf veins, becoming gray-brown with fungal sporulation, and coalescing under severe infection
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Mature lesions are rectangular, tan to gray in color, and delimited by leaf veins. Lesions are typically 1 to 4 cm long and 2 to 4 mm wide.

Holcus spot on corn appears as small, oval to irregular, white to tan lesions on the leaves, typically measuring 1–3 cm in length. The spots have a bleached or water-soaked appearance initially, then turn white or pale tan with a narrow, water-soaked to yellow-green border. Lesions are scattered across the leaf blade and may coalesce under heavy infection, giving the foliage a scorched appearance. The disease primarily affects leaf tissue and is most visible on the upper leaf surface.

Northern corn leaf blight (NCLB), caused by Exserohilum turcicum, produces large, elongated, cigar-shaped or elliptical tan to grayish-green lesions on corn leaves. Lesions typically measure 1 to 6 inches in length and run parallel to the leaf veins, with tan or straw-colored centers and wavy, irregular margins. As lesions mature, they coalesce and may cover large portions of the leaf blade, causing extensive blighting. Under humid conditions, dark olive-gray sporulation of the fungus is visible on the lesion surface, giving it a dirty or sooty appearance. Symptoms typically appear first on lower leaves and progress upward through the canopy.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Northern corn leaf blight is caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum (formerly known as Helminthosporium turcicum).

affected_organs.value: Leaves (leaf blades); husks and leaf sheaths in severe cases
affected_organs.verbatim_quote: The fungus primarily infects leaves but can also infect husks and leaf sheaths under conditions favorable for disease development.

visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Symptoms of northern corn leaf blight are cigar- or canoe-shaped lesions 1 to 6 inches long. Lesions are initially small, oval, tan spots that expand into the characteristic elongated, grayish-green to tan lesions with wavy margins that run parallel to the leaf veins. Lesions may have a dirty or sooty appearance due to dark sporulation of the fungus.

symptom_text: Gray leaf spot of corn presents as rectangular, tan to gray lesions on the leaves that are distinctly limited by leaf veins, giving them a characteristic blocky or rectangular shape. Lesions initially appear as small, necrotic spots with yellow halos that elongate parallel to the leaf veins, eventually turning gray to tan as the fungus sporulates on the lesion surface. Under humid conditions, a grayish, velvety fungal growth may be visible on lesion surfaces. Lesions are distributed across the leaf blade and can coalesce under severe infection, causing large areas of blighting that progress from lower leaves upward through the canopy.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Gray leaf spot is caused by the fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis.

affected_organs.value: Leaves (leaf blades); occasionally leaf sheaths and husks
affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Gray leaf spot lesions are most commonly found on leaves, but can also be found on leaf sheaths and husks.

visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Lesions are rectangular, tan to gray in color, and have distinct parallel edges that are limited by leaf veins. Lesions run parallel to the leaf veins.

Maize Dwarf Mosaic Virus (MDMV) produces a striking mosaic pattern on corn leaves, characterized by irregular, light green to yellow-green patches and streaks interspersed with normal dark green tissue, creating a mottled or mosaic appearance across the leaf blade. Symptoms typically appear first on young, emerging leaves near the whorl, where pale green to yellow streaking and mottle are most pronounced. As the disease progresses, infected plants may exhibit stunting, reduced plant height, and in severe cases, leaves can develop necrotic streaks or reddish-purple discoloration along the margins and midrib. Ears may be poorly filled or absent, and overall plant vigor is markedly reduced. The mosaic patterning is distributed throughout the canopy but is most vivid on younger leaves, making it a key diagnostic feature for field identification.

pathogen.value: Maize dwarf mosaic virus (MDMV), genus Potyvirus, family Potyviridae
pathogen.verbatim_quote: Maize dwarf mosaic virus (MDMV) is a member of the genus Potyvirus in the family Potyviridae.

affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Symptoms appear on leaves as a mosaic or mottle of light and dark green areas. Infected plants may be stunted and produce poorly filled ears.

visual_symptoms.value: Mosaic or mottle of light and dark green on leaves; yellow-green streaking on young leaves; stunting; necrotic streaks in severe cases
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Symptoms appear on leaves as a mosaic or mottle of light and dark green areas. In some cases, leaves may show necrotic streaking. Infected plants are often stunted.

symptom_text: Maize Lethal Necrosis (MLN) causes distinctive yellowing and necrosis beginning at the leaf margins and tips of lower leaves, progressing inward and upward to affect the entire plant. Infected plants display chlorotic mottling and streaking on leaves, followed by premature browning and drying of leaf tissue, giving a scorched or dead appearance. Necrosis spreads from the leaf edges toward the midrib, eventually killing all green tissue. Severely affected plants exhibit dead heart symptoms where the central whorl leaves die, and ears may fail to develop or show poor kernel set. The disease affects leaves, stalks, ears, and the growing point, with symptoms typically appearing across the entire canopy in advanced stages.

pathogen.value: Maize chlorotic mottle virus (MCMV) in combination with a potyvirus, most commonly Sugarcane mosaic virus (SCMV) or Wheat streak mosaic virus (WSMV)

symptom_text: Maize streak virus causes distinctive narrow, pale yellow to white streaks that run parallel to the leaf veins along the length of the leaf blade, contrasting sharply against the normal green leaf tissue. These streaks begin as small, circular to oval pale spots on young leaves near the whorl, which elongate and coalesce into continuous or broken chlorotic streaks as the leaf expands. Severely infected plants exhibit extensive yellowing of the entire leaf lamina, stunted growth, and reduced ear development. Symptoms are most pronounced on leaves that emerged after infection, with older leaves sometimes showing milder or no symptoms. The streaking pattern is distributed across all leaf surfaces of affected plants, and in severe cases the entire plant may appear pale yellow-green.

pathogen.value: Maize streak virus (MSV), genus Mastrevirus, family Geminiviridae

symptom_text: Northern leaf blight of corn is characterized by large, elongated, cigar-shaped or elliptical lesions on the leaves that are tan to grayish-green in color, typically measuring 1 to 6 inches in length. Lesions begin as small, oval, water-soaked spots that expand parallel to the leaf veins, eventually turning tan with wavy, irregular margins. Under humid conditions, dark olive-green to black sporulation of the fungus may be visible on the lesion surface, giving it a dirty or sooty appearance. Lesions are distributed across the leaf blade and can coalesce under severe infection, causing extensive blighting and premature death of leaf tissue, with lower leaves typically showing symptoms first before progressing upward through the canopy.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Northern leaf blight of corn is caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum (pass.) Leonard & Suggs (syn. Helminthosporium turcicum Pass.), the teleomorph of which is Setosphaeria turcica (Luttrell) Leonard & Suggs.

affected_organs.value: Leaves (primarily); husks and leaf sheaths in severe cases
affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Northern corn leaf blight (NCLB) affects the leaves of corn plants. In severe cases, husks and leaf sheaths may also be infected.

visual_symptoms.value: Large, elongated, cigar-shaped tan to grayish-green lesions, 1–6 inches long, with wavy margins; dark olive sporulation visible under humid conditions
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Symptoms of NCLB are long, elliptical, grayish-green or tan lesions that can measure 1 to 6 inches in length. Under humid conditions, dark olive-green sporulation may be visible on the lesions.

symptom_text: Physoderma brown spot of corn produces small, round to oval, yellow to brown spots scattered across the leaf blade, leaf sheath, and stalk. On the leaf blade, lesions appear as pale yellow or greenish-yellow flecks that later turn brown, often arranged in bands across the leaf corresponding to zones where water collects in the whorl. The midrib frequently shows dark brown to purple-black elongated lesions, which is a distinguishing characteristic of this disease. Leaf sheath lesions are dark brown to black and may cause the sheath to rot, potentially leading to stalk breakage. Affected tissue may have a water-soaked appearance initially before turning necrotic.

Common corn rust, caused by Puccinia sorghi, primarily affects the leaves of corn plants, though husks and leaf sheaths may also be involved. Symptoms appear as small, circular to elongate, powdery pustules scattered across both upper and lower leaf surfaces. Early pustules are golden-brown to cinnamon-brown in color, turning darker and more brick-red to brown as they mature and rupture through the leaf epidermis, releasing masses of powdery, rust-colored urediniospores. Pustules are typically 1–2 mm in length, raised, and randomly distributed across the leaf blade. As the season progresses, pustules may turn black as teliospores form. Severe infections can cause leaves to yellow, die prematurely, and reduce photosynthetic capacity, leading to yield loss.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Common rust of corn is caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi Schwein.

affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Pustules occur on both leaf surfaces but are also found on leaf sheaths and, occasionally, on husks.

visual_symptoms.value: Small, circular to elongate, golden-brown to brick-red powdery pustules on both leaf surfaces, turning dark brown to black with age as teliospores form
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Pustules are small, round to elongate, golden brown to brick red, and powdery. As the pustules age, they turn dark brown to black.

symptom_text: Corn smut caused by Ustilago maydis produces distinctive galls that can appear on any above-ground part of the plant, including ears, tassels, stalks, and leaves. The galls begin as white to silvery-gray, shiny, fleshy swellings covered by a thin membrane. As the galls mature, they enlarge dramatically—sometimes reaching the size of a softball—and the interior fills with a mass of dark olive-brown to black powdery teliospores. The outer membrane eventually ruptures, releasing the sooty black spore mass. On ears, individual kernels may be replaced by these tumor-like galls, while on tassels and stalks the galls appear as irregular, distorted swellings. The contrast between the early white-silver exterior and the later black spore mass makes this disease highly recognizable in the field.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Corn smut is caused by the fungus Ustilago maydis (DC) Corda.

affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Galls can form on any above ground part of the plant including the ear, tassel, stalk, and leaves.

visual_symptoms.value: White to silvery-gray galls that mature to dark olive-brown or black powdery spore masses; galls can reach softball size; individual kernels replaced by tumor-like swellings
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Galls are white to silvery gray and shiny when young. As galls mature, they become filled with a dark, olive-brown to black powdery mass of spores. The outer membrane eventually ruptures, releasing the spores.

symptom_text: Southern corn leaf blight, caused by Cochliobolus heterostrophus (anamorph: Bipolaris maydis), produces tan to brown, elongated or rectangular lesions on corn leaves that are typically limited in width by the leaf veins, giving them a characteristic oblong shape with tan centers and darker brown borders. Lesions range from about 1 to 3 cm in length and may coalesce under heavy disease pressure, causing large areas of leaf tissue to die and turn a straw-brown color. In susceptible genotypes, lesions can also appear on leaf sheaths, husks, and ear shanks. Under humid conditions, olive-gray sporulation of the pathogen may be visible on lesion surfaces. Severe infections result in blighting of entire leaves, premature senescence, and significant yield loss.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Southern corn leaf blight is caused by the fungus Cochliobolus heterostrophus (Drechsler) Drechsler (anamorph: Bipolaris maydis (Nisikado & Miyake) Shoemaker).

affected_organs.value: Leaves, leaf sheaths, husks, ear shanks
affected_organs.verbatim_quote: The fungus can infect leaves, leaf sheaths, husks, and ear shanks.

visual_symptoms.value: Tan to brown, elongated rectangular lesions limited by leaf veins, with tan centers and brown borders, ranging 1–3 cm in length, coalescing under heavy pressure
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Lesions are tan to brown, rectangular in shape, and limited in width by the leaf veins. Lesions range from 1 to 3 cm in length and have tan centers with brown borders.

symptom_text: Southern rust of corn produces small, circular to oval pustules (uredinia) that are densely packed and predominantly found on the upper leaf surface, though they may also appear on lower leaf surfaces, husks, and leaf sheaths. The pustules are pale orange to tan or cinnamon-brown in color, distinctly lighter and more orange than the brick-red pustules of common rust. Pustules rupture through the epidermis and release powdery, orange-colored urediniospores. Lesions are typically concentrated on the upper canopy leaves and can coalesce under heavy infection, causing large areas of the leaf to appear orange and powdery. Severely infected leaves may yellow and die prematurely, leading to significant reductions in photosynthetic area.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Southern rust is caused by the fungus Puccinia polysora Underw.

affected_organs.value: Leaves (primarily upper surface), leaf sheaths, husks
affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Pustules are found primarily on the upper leaf surface but can also be found on lower leaf surfaces, husks, and leaf sheaths.

visual_symptoms.value: Small, circular to oval, orange to tan pustules densely clustered on upper leaf surfaces, releasing powdery orange spores
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Pustules of southern rust are smaller, more circular, and more orange in color than those of common rust. They are densely packed on the upper leaf surface and produce powdery, orange urediniospores.

symptom_text: Stewart's disease of corn, caused by the bacterium Pantoea stewartii, produces two distinct phases of symptoms. During the seedling (wilt) phase, young plants exhibit rapid wilting and death, with leaves showing pale green to yellow streaks that run parallel to the leaf veins. In the leaf blight phase, which occurs on older plants, irregular, water-soaked lesions with wavy or irregular margins develop on the leaves, turning pale green to yellow and then tan or brown as they dry out. These elongated, straw-colored streaks with wavy, irregular margins are distributed along the length of the leaf blade and have a characteristic 'scorched' appearance. Infected vascular tissue may appear discolored when stalks are cut, and in susceptible sweet corn hybrids, the pathogen can cause systemic infection leading to stunting and poor ear development.

affected_organs.value: Leaves, spreading from flea beetle feeding scars

visual_symptoms.value: Pale green to yellow streaks spreading from flea beetle scars, browning as tissue dies, with wavy margins following the veins
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Stewart's disease lesions spread from flea beetle feeding scars (a tiny scratch on the leaf) and are initially pale green to yellow streaks, later becoming brown as tissue dies. The margins of the streaks are usually wavy but generally follow leaf veins.

symptom_text: Tar spot of corn is characterized by numerous small, raised, circular to oval black stromata (fungal fruiting bodies) scattered across the upper and lower surfaces of leaves, leaf sheaths, and husks. These tar-like spots are typically 0.5–2 mm in diameter, have a shiny, black, slightly raised texture that cannot be rubbed off, and are distributed irregularly across the leaf blade. In severe infections, lesions may be surrounded by tan to brown necrotic halos, forming a 'fisheye' pattern. Heavy sporulation causes large portions of the leaf surface to appear blackened, leading to premature senescence and significant yield loss.

visual_symptoms.value: Small raised black stromata scattered over both leaf surfaces; tan-to-brown 'fisheye' lesions with dark borders may surround them
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Tar spot appears as small, raised, black spots scattered across the upper and lower leaf surfaces.
